A recent study has looked at what happens when students take notes by hand and when they take notes on a laptop. The researchers asked students to watch the same short lecture, and then tested them on what they had understood.
The students who typed wrote far more words — in some cases almost everything the speaker said — while those who wrote by hand wrote about a third less. That did not matter when the test asked for simple facts: on those questions, the two groups did about the same. It mattered a great deal when the test asked students to explain ideas. There, the handwriting group did clearly better.
The researchers think the reason is not the pen itself. When you write by hand, you cannot keep up with the speaker, so you have to decide what matters and put it in your own words. Typing, by contrast, invites you to copy the lecture word for word without ever deciding what is important.
One detail is worth remembering. When the students with laptops were told, before the lecture, not to write everything down, the two groups performed almost the same. In other words, the machine is not the problem; the way we use it is. The researchers suggest that students who take a laptop to a lecture should treat it as a tool for thinking, not as a machine for recording.

A city in the north of England is to keep its libraries open until nine in the evening from next month. The decision follows a six-month trial, during which evening visits by students and by people who work late rose sharply. The city council says the longer hours will be paid for by a small increase in parking charges, and that the money for new books will not be touched. Library staff will also run free classes in basic computer skills twice a week. A council spokesperson said the aim was to make the library “the warmest and quietest room in the neighbourhood”. The council expects more than twenty thousand extra visits over the coming year.
